```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(easyNIS)
```

## Use the synthetic fixture

`nis_example()` creates an invented Parquet dataset with familiar NIS fields.
It is suitable for learning and examples, not for estimating national
quantities.

```{r fixture}
path <- nis_example(years = 2019:2020)
nis <- nis_open(path)
nis |> dplyr::count(YEAR) |> dplyr::collect()
```

The result reports the number of synthetic rows in each selected year.

easyNIS does not bundle real NIS data. The HCUP [Nationwide Data Use Agreement](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/team/NationwideDUA.jsp)
advises avoiding publication of values of 1–10 in text and tables. Separately,
the [Checklist for Working with the NIS](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/db/nation/nis/nischecklist.jsp)
says at least two hospitals must contribute to each cell. `nis_suppress()` masks counts at or below `threshold` (10 by default), applies
complementary suppression by default for data frames, and, when given hospital
counts from `nis_cell_counts()`, masks cells from fewer than two hospitals. Use
`nis_example()` to try the workflow without
licensed data.

## Select years and columns

`years` limits which annual files are opened. Use `dplyr::select()` to narrow
what a later collection needs; lazy operations are evaluated when collected.

```{r columns}
nis_open(path, years = 2020) |>
  dplyr::select(YEAR, AGE, FEMALE, LOS) |>
  dplyr::collect() |>
  head()
```

The preview contains only the requested variables from the synthetic 2020
file. Mixed-case column names are normalized to upper case; already lower-case
names remain unchanged.

## Annual release checks

`nis_open()` checks converted Core files by default. DuckDB compares the row
count, sum of `DISCWT`, and distinct `HOSP_NIS` count for each year against
HCUP's Core Weighted and Hospital Weights summary statistics for 2012–2024.
[HCUP NIS summary statistics](https://hcup-us.ahrq.gov/db/nation/nis/nissummstats.jsp)

When those fields are present, missing `YEAR`, `YEAR` outside the opened
years, and nonpositive `NIS_STRATUM` values also warn.
Warnings leave the lazy query available. Files from `nis_example()` still
undergo these integrity checks and are excluded from the published totals.
If you open an intentional extract, set `check_release = FALSE` to skip the
check.

## Filter and project before collecting

`nis_open()` uses DuckDB's native Parquet reader by default and returns a lazy
dbplyr table. `duckdb`, `dbplyr`, and `DBI` are required dependencies. Filter
and select before collecting when later analysis needs an in-memory data
frame. The default reader is unchanged; `reader = "arrow"` opts in to the
optional `arrow` package for reading Parquet files individually.

```{r duckdb}
duck <- nis_open(path, years = 2020)
duck |> dplyr::count(YEAR) |> dplyr::collect()
```

This count is the same synthetic year summary, evaluated through DuckDB.

Arrow preserves source bytes in string columns, including malformed UTF-8
bytes. It does not repair or automatically detect every invalid string, and
malformed values may still fail in downstream string operations. Validate or
repair text before analysis when those operations are needed.

When converting HCUP ASCII files to Parquet, declare the source encoding so
string values are written as valid UTF-8. For example, convert Latin-1 text to
UTF-8 rather than writing bytes under the wrong encoding label.

## Common pitfalls

> **Common pitfalls**
>
> - Opening all years and collecting all columns can require substantial
>   memory. Filter and select before collecting.
> - Survey-design preparation collects the selected design fields in R. Keep
>   the cohort and retained columns bounded before using `nis_design()`.
> - `nis_example()` data are invented and should not be reported as NIS
>   estimates.

See [Cohort definitions](cohorts.html), [`nis_open()`](../reference/nis_open.html),
and [`nis_example()`](../reference/nis_example.html).

## Working with data larger than RAM

DuckDB scans the Parquet files in place. Filter rows and select fields on the
lazy query. Then collect a small summary, or write a large result directly to
a private Parquet file. `nis_design()` still needs enough R memory for the
selected cohort, retained variables, and survey design. Use a narrow `keep`
to limit that cost. [DuckDB COPY statement](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/statements/copy)

Set DuckDB options before calling `nis_open()`. This example uses a low thread
count and places spill files on a private disk. Choose the memory and spill
budgets for your machine and available disk space.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
options(easyNIS.duckdb_config = list(
  memory_limit = "4GB",
  threads = 2L,
  temp_directory = tempdir(),
  max_temp_directory_size = "40GB"
))
query <- nis_open(data_path, years = 2019:2022)
query |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 18) |>
  dplyr::group_by(YEAR) |>
  dplyr::summarise(discharge_count = dplyr::n()) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

To write a result on disk, set `private_parquet_path` to a file in your private
output directory and send the lazy query to DuckDB.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
projection <- query |>
  dplyr::filter(AGE >= 18) |>
  dplyr::select(YEAR, AGE)
connection <- dbplyr::remote_con(projection)
statement <- dbplyr::sql_render(projection)
destination <- DBI::dbQuoteString(connection, private_parquet_path)
DBI::dbExecute(connection,
  paste0("COPY (", statement, ") TO ", destination, " (FORMAT PARQUET)"))
```

Use `preserve_insertion_order = FALSE` for memory-constrained scans or exports
whose result order is immaterial. Use an explicit sort when you need a defined
order. DuckDB's memory limit controls its buffer manager. R objects and some
DuckDB operations can use additional memory. See the
[DuckDB workload tuning guide](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/guides/performance/how_to_tune_workloads).

Reuse a query for related summaries so they share one connection. The memory
and spill settings apply to each open connection. When an analysis finishes,
discard the query and any lazy tables derived from it. Garbage collection
releases the connection and removes its spill directory. In a loop that opens
many datasets, release each completed query before opening the next one if
disk or memory is tight.
